topic: Laya: offline OS for Jev on Mac M4 CoreML, 45 decisions per second
keyword: laya jev os mac m4 coreml offline
verdict_headline: The 45 decisions/second figure is real but measured on M3 Max, not M4, and it is an average of an uncapped loop -- not a guaranteed sustained rate. The M4 pairing came from a 4-line install gist title, not from a benchmark.

competitors.publisher: mizorewww (the Core ML port author; 1,517 stars, 125 forks, Apache-2.0, created 2026-09-19, last push 2026-09-22)
key_points: Primary source: Laya ported to Apple Core ML + Neural Engine, zero generated tokens, offline after one weight download.
Sustained 49.1-50.0 decisions/s (pooled 49.66/s) across three uncapped 600-step Snake episodes on M3 Max 40-core GPU, 128 GiB, macOS 27.2, zero deaths, two safety interventions.
Separate single-question microbenchmark: ANE FP16 4.98 ms P50 / 5.31 ms P95; W8 variant 4.88 / 5.23 ms.
Against its own compiled MLX FP16 baseline: 1.39x faster and 2.78x better whole-system energy per decision (W8: 1.42x / 3.19x). Author states plainly the requested 10x target was NOT achieved.

Paced sweep shows the ceiling is pacing-dependent: 20 req/s passes (18.4 observed, 0.67% deadline misses); 30/40/50/60 req/s all FAIL, with 44.21 observed at the 50 req/s setting and 53.33% deadline misses.

Honest limits: ANE bundle is capped at 96 total tokens (question + options + state), Core ML build takes 3.4-4.2 s with a 313-475 ms first prediction, and Core ML CPU+GPU remains the recommended default -- a plain SDPA export is SLOWER than MLX; only the ANE graph rewrite wins.
Fidelity fixtures: three general checkpoints match upstream on 189/189 validation questions; ANE FP16 L96 passes 59/59 with max probability drift 0.002925.

competitors.publisher: fordnox, 2026-09-20 (34 stars, 4 forks, 4 comments) -- the origin of the M4 headline
key_points: Contains only four shell commands: uv init, uv add 'laya-coreml[demo]', hf download the ANE bundle, run the Snake demo.
The 'Mac m4 CoreML Offline' phrasing lives in the gist description; the gist publishes no M4 benchmark of any kind.
The only measurement in the thread is a /usr/bin/sample memory dump: 560.4M physical footprint, 778.0M peak, macOS 27.0.
HN thread (item 49777106) reached 178 points; the author concedes in comments that 'maybe OS Jev is too strong of a wording'.
Commenter ImJasonH reports an iPhone 15 Pro one-shot of the same weights deciding in ~40 ms -- a stronger portability signal than the M4 claim.

competitors.publisher: gazelle93, 7 systems benchmarked, 200 items per domain, pre-registered pass/fail rules
key_points: The strongest counterweight to Laya hype: at 128 candidates Jev scores 60% where Laya scores 39% and the best other open model 41%.
Laya loses -0.073 accuracy per doubling of the option list versus Jev's -0.043 -- third-worst of seven systems.
Laya changes its answer on 49.4% of decisions when option order is shuffled (Jev 14.6%); with order fixed both are 0.0%.
Laya loses -0.351 accuracy when distractors become plausible versus Jev's -0.105.
Conclusion quoted: Laya is the weaker implementation of a real idea, and a single-number benchmark hides this because at K=2 Laya trails Jev by only two points.

competitors.publisher: James Cruce, The Geek Learns, Sep 22 2026
key_points: Production deployment account on a Mac Studio M3 Ultra / 256 GB, local-only, with a FastAPI service exposing TypeSafe's exact wire shape on 127.0.0.1:8017.
Chose Laya over Jev for privacy and control, not cost -- explicitly refuses to quote a break-even number for the hardware.

Key operational design: Laya only ranks pre-filtered survivors (max 5 plus an abstain option); permission never comes from the model, and the gateway re-validates the returned option, confidence and margin.
Fails closed: refuses to download at inference time, rejects over-budget token requests instead of letting the runtime silently truncate, caps Choice at 20 options, serializes inference.

Warns the model card itself says the model is overconfident and needs domain-specific calibration; confidence is entropy-derived, not a success probability. One use case (post-failure recovery) failed acceptance and was disabled.

The architectural counter-argument: an off-the-shelf LLM (GLM-5.3-Flash) can be prompted into single-forward-pass typed decisions with per-option probabilities, reaching parity with Jev on decision accuracy and speed.
The exploit: the JSON shape is already known, so only the typed judgement tokens need to be read from the logits -- no autoregressive JSON generation.
Adds image-based typed decisions, which Jev cannot do.
Frames specialized decision models as a latency/cost optimization over prompting, not a capability class of their own.
The memory-constrained alternative to Core ML: M5 Pro, 32 ms median latency at 2.11 GiB peak RSS, or 171 ms at 0.74 GiB in minimal mode (streams layers from disk).
All three memory settings matched exactly on 260/260 decisions including probabilities -- a useful correctness control.
~843 MB model download, Apple Silicon M1+, macOS 14+.

angles: Fact-check frame: the headline bundles three separate claims -- 'Mac M4', 'CoreML offline' and '45 decisions/second'. Only the offline CoreML part is backed by the repo; the M4 label is a gist title and the 45/s number is an M3 Max average.

Why 45 is the tell: 49.66/s uncapped on M3 Max and 44.21/s observed at a 50/s requested rate are two different things. Rounding down to 45 quietly converts an uncapped average into what reads like a guaranteed sustained rate -- and the paced table shows only 20/s actually holds a deadline.

What actually changed: no new weights, no retraining. Six runtimes (MLX, Core ML/ANE, browser WASM, Node, Android LiteRT, edge NPU) in roughly 72 hours by different people moving the same 322M/421M weights. The port is the story, not the model.

The honest-engineering angle, which is rare and worth praising: the port author publishes his own failed 10x target, a failing paced sweep, CPU-plan attribution showing the Neural Engine was never preferred in the plain export, and 6-bit/4-bit experiments rejected at the fidelity gate.

The calibration trap: the shipped choice:11+ temperature bucket of 0.1006 gets clamped to 0.5-5.0 because it would have reported a coin flip as near-certainty. Anyone shipping this should read agent.temperature_raw and not trust the surface confidence.

The 'offline' asterisk: offline is true after first download, but you need Core ML compiled on first load (3.4-4.2 s), Apple Silicon with macOS 15+, Python 3.11-3.13, and the ANE bundle is capped at 96 tokens -- so 'your OS runs on Jev offline' oversells what fits in the budget.

Under-pressure reality check: the same openness that makes Laya easy to run locally also means it degrades faster than Jev as the option list grows. Use it for bounded, low-cardinality, order-stable decisions and treat it as a recommender, never as permission.

verification_notes: M4 claim: NOT verifiable. No M4 benchmark exists in the laya-coreml repo. Every headline measurement is M3 Max (40-core GPU, 128 GiB, macOS 27.2). The M4 label originates in the gist description 'Laya on Mac m4 CoreML Offline'.

45 decisions/second: PARTIALLY verifiable. Matches neither headline number exactly. Closest published values are 49.1-50.0/s (uncapped, M3 Max) and 44.21/s (observed at a requested 50/s, which failed the deadline test with 53.33% misses).
Offline operation: VERIFIED. Weights download once, then inference needs no PyTorch, MLX or Transformers and no network; the sibling MPS port states inference works offline after first run.

Speedup over Jev (~10x): FROM A VENDOR-ADJACENT SOURCE. The 10.4x average claim comes from the Laya project's own comparison table against TypeSafe's published Jev numbers, not from a head-to-head run on identical hardware.

Methodology caveats worth repeating in the article: energy figures are whole-system estimates with sensor and background-load uncertainty; the M5 Max vs M4 Pro cross-backend bench in the wild is a two-form-factor comparison, so thermal headroom is a confound.
